articles.title: Flat optics roadmap charts path toward smaller imaging and sensing systems
articles.dek: For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size.
paragraphs: For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size. Today, advances in nanotechnology are enabling a different approach. Researchers can now engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light, creating ultrathin optical components that offer new ways to control how light behaves.

A new roadmap published in the Journal of Nanophotonics examines the rapid evolution of optical meta-devices and outlines the developments that could shape the field in the coming years. This roadmap, led by a team at City University of Hong Kong and RIKEN Center for Advanced Photonics, surveys progress in metamaterials and metasurfaces, technologies that are helping transform optical systems from assemblies of bulky components into compact, multifunctional devices.

Metasurfaces consist of carefully designed arrays of nanoscale structures that can manipulate the phase, amplitude and polarization of light. Because these capabilities can be incorporated into ultrathin, planar optical elements, metasurfaces offer an alternative to many traditional optical components. This shift toward flat optics could enable smaller and lighter imaging, sensing and communication systems.

Among the most active areas of research are metalenses, flat optical devices that focus light without the curved glass used in conventional lenses. The roadmap highlights recent advances in metalens performance and their integration into compact imaging systems, reflecting ongoing efforts to simplify conventional optical assemblies and develop more compact optical systems.

The roadmap also points to artificial intelligence and inverse-design techniques as increasingly important tools for developing future metadevices. Designing nanoscale optical structures involves navigating an enormous number of possible geometries. Data-driven approaches are helping researchers identify designs that would be difficult to discover through conventional methods alone, while improving performance and reducing development time.

Another major area of progress charted by the roadmap involves reconfigurable metasurfaces . By combining metasurfaces with tunable materials and microelectromechanical systems, researchers are creating devices whose optical properties can be adjusted after fabrication. Such systems could support adaptive imaging and sensing technologies capable of responding to changing conditions in real time.

The roadmap further explores advances in nonlinear optics, ultrasensitive sensing, holography, augmented and virtual reality displays, and quantum imaging. Increasingly, metasurfaces are being integrated with detectors, emitters and other active components, bringing the technology closer to practical optical systems rather than standalone laboratory demonstrations.

Corresponding author Din Ping Tsai notes, "While significant technical challenges remain, particularly in large-scale manufacturing and system integration, the field is witnessing steady progress toward fabrication methods compatible with established semiconductor processes." The roadmap identifies scalable production and integration as key steps for translating research advances into commercial optical technologies.

By bringing together developments across multiple areas of research, the roadmap presents a snapshot of a field moving from fundamental discovery toward real-world implementation. As advances in materials, design and manufacturing continue to converge, optical meta-devices are expected to play an increasingly important role in next-generation imaging, sensing, communications and quantum technologies.

articles.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
articles.dek: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of…
paragraphs: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

At its core, the puzzle is a speed limit. A black hole grows by swallowing, or accreting, gas, but the infalling matter heats up and shines, and the radiation pushes on the gas still arriving. At the so-called Eddington limit, radiation pressure balances gravity and infall cannot speed up further. Because this limit scales with the black hole's mass, growth is exponential. If, as usually assumed, about 10% of the infalling mass is converted to radiation, the mass grows by a factor of e (about 2. 7) every 45 million years.

A stellar-mass black hole of about a hundred solar masses would need about 17 such steps, roughly 770 million years, to reach 3 billion solar masses. When you account for the time it took for the stellar black holes to form, the universe had less than 600 million years available.

There are two popular ways out. One is to start with a "heavy seed" of at least 10,000 solar masses, formed by the direct collapse of enormous gas clouds. This would skip the slowest part of the climb. The other is to break the Eddington limit: If the energy released by infalling gas is removed in ways other than radiation, the black hole can grow far faster. Both options have caveats: Direct collapse requires a rare combination of conditions, and it is uncertain whether real accretion flows can stay super-Eddington for hundreds of millions of years.

In a new paper with my colleague Matas Tartėnas, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics , we ask whether a third, older and simpler idea survives confrontation with the latest data. It is called chaotic accretion, and it needs neither a heavy seed nor a broken speed limit.

The "chaos" in our model comes from how gas reaches the black hole. We consider a slowly rotating dark matter halo, so that gas falls in from essentially random directions. Each stream forms a small disk, tilted randomly relative to the black hole's spin, feeds it briefly and is quickly followed by another, tilted differently. Some episodes spin the black hole up; others, where the disk counter-rotates, spin it down. Spin-down is rarer but more efficient per unit of mass, so over time the spin stays low.

That matters because a slowly spinning black hole converts less of the infalling mass into light: It radiates away only about 6 to 7. 5% of the mass it swallows, rather than 10%. This may seem like a small difference, but it shortens the growth timescale from 45 to roughly 27–32 million years, and the time required to grow J0313-1806 from 770 to 550 million years.

In this scenario, the gas supply on large scales can exceed the rate necessary for the Eddington limit. What matters, though, is how much material reaches the event horizon, and that stays near the Eddington rate, while most of the rest is removed along the way. The large gas reservoir, however, ensures that the black hole may be fed nearly continuously.

We compared this prediction with mass estimates for all known supermassive black holes at redshifts above seven. The most reliable (virial) estimates, out to redshift 10. 6 and including J0313-1806, can all be explained by a seed of about 100 solar masses or smaller, formed around 100 million years after the Big Bang, growing on a timescale of about 32 million years. This requires almost continuous feeding at least 85% of the time at the Eddington rate, or all the time at 85% of it.

This shows that the scenario works, not that the alternatives fail. Our scenario cannot explain several existing mass estimates, but those are made using methods that rely on more assumptions about the accretion flow. For example, for the galaxy GN-z11, the virial estimate is about seven times lower than the less robust one. Several more distant black holes lack robust masses and would make excellent near-future observation targets.

Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

A study by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, explores how workers use technology to report workplace concerns and finds there is a lot of gray space between informal conversations and formal reporting. In a paper published in the Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction , the scholars introduce the concept of buffer spaces, which sit between informal and formal workplace conflict resolution and can offer a path toward resolution.
The study won a best paper award at the 2026 ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing.

"When workplace concerns don't get reported, they don't just disappear," said Peiyao Liu, a doctoral student in computational media and the study's lead author. "They build up, and people get burned out. Understanding how people actually decide whether to speak up matters for everyone, not just the person with the problem."

Liu carried out this research with associate professor of computational media Norman Su, who leads the Authentic User Experience Lab at the Baskin School of Engineering, and associate professor Lynn Dombrowski at Georgia Tech's School of Interactive Computing. Su's group studies the relationship of technology with subcultures, using methods like interviews and surveys to better understand people's pain points with technology in everyday life and offer design guidelines.
"We want to offer some direction for future researchers to think about why current channels or technology don't work, and how we can design the tools to support them," Liu said.
Su and Liu are interested in workplace concern reporting because it's a widespread and often painful issue, but one that can be particularly challenging for people with marginalized identities.

"The people who stay quiet are always the ones who need help the most—women in male-dominated teams, LGBTQ employees, people of color or people with disabilities," Liu said. "For them, speaking up can feel riskier."

The researchers, who are based at the UC Santa Cruz Silicon Valley Campus, set out to better understand how employees and HR professionals use formal systems, backchannel conversations and everything in between to resolve issues. They partnered with the Bay Area Human Resources Executives Council, which holds meetings at the Silicon Valley Campus, to learn and get feedback on their work.

Past research on workplace reporting tends to focus on the two far ends of the reporting spectrum: staying silent and filing formal complaints. But in interviews with 22 participants, including 10 employees from various industries and 12 HR professionals, the researchers found people's real experiences tend to fall somewhere in between.

People may turn to conversations in person, on messaging platforms like Slack or on social media for comfort, validation and support, but this may not always lead to real solutions. Meanwhile, formal reporting resources can be seen as untrustworthy, difficult to use and ultimately ineffective, and workers may fear retribution.

articles.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
articles.dek: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical…
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

New University of Bristol research published in Scientific Reports on Nov. 16 has found large language models were able to check research applications against published standards within minutes—however, performance varied significantly between models.

The study, conducted in collaboration with the Health Research Authority (HRA), tested three widely used large language models (Claude 3. 5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-4o and Microsoft Copilot) on a task that currently requires substantial human time: checking research ethics applications against the HRA's published quality standards.

The results showed significant differences between the tools. Claude achieved fully correct answers to 87. 9% of checks, compared with 66. 5% for ChatGPT and 62. 8% for Copilot. It was also the fastest, taking an average of just over seven minutes to assess each application.
The findings suggest AI could help reduce the administrative burden associated with research approvals, allowing staff to devote more time to the ethical questions that require human judgment.

Lead author Dr. Panos Maghsoudlou, NIHR academic clinical lecturer in ophthalmology in the School of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences, said: "These results highlight both the potential of AI-assisted checking and the risks of relying on its outputs without verification.

"Large language models could be used to support the early stages of the research approval process, identifying missing information and potential departures from published standards before applications reach an ethics committee. By automating routine checks, AI could help reduce administrative workloads and enable approvals staff and committee members to concentrate on the substantive ethical issues at the heart of research review."
Before a research study can begin, its application must undergo checks which can involve reviewing hundreds of pages and comparing information across multiple documents.

Although essential, these types of tasks can be time-consuming and account for a significant proportion of the approval process. The new study examined whether large language models could undertake these checks, comparing their accuracy, speed and response quality, as well as the types of errors they made.
All three models were able to carry out checks against the HRA's quality standards, but their performance varied considerably.

Claude answered every question and completed each application in an average of seven minutes. ChatGPT took an average of 13 minutes, while Copilot took 23 minutes. Copilot also failed to answer data protection questions in most applications.

The differences were particularly striking when the models were assessed on their ability to identify problems requiring correction. Claude identified an average of eight errors per application, compared with 2. 3 for ChatGPT and 1. 3 for Copilot.

There were also differences in how well the LLMs performed. Failures in logical reasoning were the most common source of inaccurate responses across all three models. Claude produced fewer hallucinations —instances in which an AI system generates information that is incorrect or unsupported—than the other tools.

articles.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
articles.dek: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem.
paragraphs: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

In a study recently published in ACS Nano , researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and their collaborators propose "flipping engineering," a new way to design layered materials that readily conduct heat along their layers while strongly blocking heat flow between them.

In three-dimensional integrated circuits , semiconductor chips are stacked vertically. This can cause heat to build up between the layers and travel from high-power computing chips into neighboring components such as memory. To prevent this, engineers need materials that act like a radiator in one direction and an insulating blanket in the other.

"Our approach uses Janus atomic layers, whose two faces consist of different atomic species," says lead author of the study Xin Wu. "Because the top and bottom are different, we can choose the orientation of each stacked layer individually, right side up or upside down, almost like a game of Tetris. This gives us a simple, programmable switch for designing the structure."

The team focused on MoSSe, a molybdenum-based material with sulfur atoms on one face and selenium atoms on the other. A 14-layer stack can be arranged in 8,192 different flipping sequences, far too many to test individually. Instead, the researchers built a machine-learning workflow combining thermal transport prediction with stacking optimization to find the best candidate.

After evaluating only about 3% of the possible configurations, they identified a structure whose in-plane thermal conductivity is approximately 760 times its effective cross-plane thermal conductivity at room temperature. This thermal anisotropy ratio is about 35% higher than that of an ordered crystalline stack of the same thickness.

"The irregular flipping sequence disrupts the vibrations that carry heat between the layers," explains senior author Masahiro Nomura. "Importantly, it leaves the vibrations that carry heat along the layers essentially untouched, so we can selectively suppress cross-plane heat transport while largely preserving in-plane thermal conductivity."

Although fabrication and experimental validation remain challenges for the future, existing layer-by-layer assembly techniques, including methods that can flip individual layers, offer a possible route to building such structures. The findings provide a new material design principle that could help improve thermal management in three-dimensional semiconductor chips.

articles.title: Earth’s Ancient Oceans May Have Fooled Scientists About the Rise of Oxygen
articles.dek: Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.
paragraphs: Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.

For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it a vastly different world from the one that supports complex life today. New research suggests oxygen accumulated in three major stages, with the deep ocean taking hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

Two geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology argue in The Innovation that scientists may have misjudged the timing of Earth’s oxygenation by using ancient ocean chemistry to estimate atmospheric conditions. Ocean chemistry is also influenced by nutrients, biological activity, circulation, and basin shape, making it an imperfect record of the air.

Instead, the researchers examined an oxygen isotope signature preserved in sedimentary sulfate. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide produce a distinctive shortage of oxygen-17 in the atmosphere. This signature enters sulfate when sulfide minerals weather, providing a record of atmospheric oxygen.
The first major increase, the Great Oxidation Event, occurred between 2. 4 billion and 2. 1 billion years ago, raising oxygen from less than one-millionth of today’s level to between 0. 1% and 10%.

The next increases occurred between 1. 3 billion and 1. 0 billion years ago and between 440 million and 410 million years ago, earlier than traditionally thought. The better-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, dated to 800 million to 500 million and 420 million to 360 million years ago, may instead reflect ocean responses that lagged behind atmospheric changes by roughly 200 million and 30 million years.

Oxygen nevertheless remained scarce. Models based on the isotope evidence place mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at just 0. 1% to 1% of modern levels. Charcoal, which requires roughly three-quarters of today’s oxygen concentration to form during burning, first appears around 420 million years ago.

Atmospheric and ocean oxygen generally increased together over billion-year timescales, although they could move in opposite directions over millions of years. When oxygen entered seawater containing accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, chemical reactions consumed the gas and could lower atmospheric levels. Some geological signals previously interpreted as oxygen increases may therefore indicate declines.

Oxygen also spread unevenly through the oceans. Photosynthetic microbes created localized oxygen-rich environments as early as 3 billion years ago, or earlier. These dominated during the Archean, before oxygen supplied from the atmosphere became increasingly important. The ocean interior did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago.

For life, the transition was gradual. An oxygen-free atmosphere severely limited organisms dependent on the gas, while fluctuating levels during the Proterozoic opened new habitats as animals evolved. After the third atmospheric increase, greater oxygen availability helped support larger bodies, active predation, and expansion into deeper waters.

The researchers caution that the isotope record has limited time resolution, oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain poorly constrained, and additional increases may have gone undetected. Their findings suggest that Earth’s transformation into an oxygen-rich world was shaped not only by rising atmospheric levels, but also by the long delay before oxygen reached the ocean depths.

articles.title: New analysis shows that even young children want to be seen as morally good
articles.dek: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .
paragraphs: By continuing with Google, Facebook or Apple, you agree to the Terms of Use .

As early as 130,000 years ago, the first human societies were built on morality and cooperation within groups. The same is true today. Even young children exhibit a distinctly human desire to be seen as morally good. That is the conclusion of a new article by researchers at Leipzig University. Humboldt Research Fellow Dr. Leon Li and Junior Professor Dr. Sebastian Grüneisen are investigating the origins of human cooperation and social identity. Their paper, "Evolutionary foundations of social identity," has just been published in the journal Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences .

The traditional psychological definition of social identity describes how people see themselves as members of a group. Building on this definition, Li and Grüneisen argue that the first group early humans identified with was their own cultural group. The earliest form of social identity therefore involved seeing oneself as a good, norm-abiding member of that group.

Over the past two years, the researchers have analyzed several behavioral studies on this subject. The findings suggest that children respect the social norms of their own group and favor it over other groups. Even very young children are aware of the knowledge they share with other members of their group and feel a sense of responsibility for the group's actions.

"Human cooperation develops in two stages—both on an evolutionary level and as individual children develop," explains developmental psychologist Dr. Leon Li, the article's lead author. Initially, humans develop the ability to cooperate with specific individuals they know through direct experience. In the second stage, they become capable of 'cooperating' with the group as a whole—including members they may never have met.

"What is new about our work is that we offer an evolutionary explanation for how social identity emerged in human cognition," says Grüneisen. While considerable research over the past few decades has focused on social identity from a psychological perspective, its evolutionary origins have received relatively little attention. To investigate these origins, the psychologists analyzed a range of comparative studies—including studies comparing great apes and human children—as well as developmental studies examining children's behavior in social contexts.

"Social identity is undoubtedly a prominent topic in public debate today. Exploring the fundamental aspects of social identity could help people gain a clearer understanding of what they actually mean when they talk about it," explains Li. He believes further research is needed to determine whether children conform to social norms out of a genuine, internalized respect for their group's norms or whether they are simply motivated by a strategic desire to maintain a good reputation among other group members.

articles.title: Rewriting History: New Research Reveals Ancient Iron Age King May Have Been a Woman
articles.dek: A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.
paragraphs: A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.

Research led by Dr. Miles Russell at Bournemouth University (BU) challenges the traditional identification of Verica as a male king. Drawing on the ruler’s name and coin imagery, Russell argues that a woman held a central role in the events leading to Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, whose lands covered much of modern-day Hampshire and West Sussex. Driven from power around AD 40, the ruler fled to Emperor Claudius in Rome, seeking support. That appeal gave Claudius an opportunity to intervene in Britain and claim a military triumph.

Russell, BU’s Director of Archaeological Fieldwork, argues that Verica’s identity has been filtered through assumptions made by earlier historians. “Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.”

One clue, he suggests, is the name itself. Its “a” ending also appears in the names of female rulers from the same period, including Cartimandua of the Brigantes (in Yorkshire) and Boudica of the Iceni (in Norfolk). Boudica’s revolt against Roman rule in AD 60 made her the most famous of the three, but Russell considers Verica the more powerful and influential figure.

The title on Verica’s coins has also shaped how the ruler is remembered. “People also assume she was a ‘he’ because of the term ‘rex’ on coins, but ‘rex’ is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous,” Russell said. “The use of the Latin title ‘rex’ on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.”

For Russell, the images offer another important clue: “Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.”

Verica’s identity also changes how Russell interprets the Roman account of the invasion. Historian Cassius Dio claimed that Claudius crossed the Channel because Verica persuaded him to do so. That story fits a broader pattern in Roman writing, which portrayed Claudius as weak-minded and ineffective, with women and freed slaves directing his decisions.

“The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked,” Russell said. “In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica’s role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her onboard ensured the project was a success as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.”

In this interpretation, Verica offered both a political justification for invasion and practical help in carrying it out. As Russell put it, “The invasion was Claudius’ great triumph, it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.”

Russell argues that Verica deserves recognition among Britain’s earliest influential female leaders. “We should take the archaeological evidence at face value,” he said, “and remember Verica as a female king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed and fled to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.”

The work follows earlier BU research into women’s place in Iron Age society. Published last year, that research involved Russell and university colleagues and found evidence of communities centered on women, where husbands moved to live with their wives’ communities.
The argument about Verica is presented in Caratacus: Great King of Britain , published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902), and discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology .

articles.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
articles.dek: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University
paragraphs: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University

During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated. Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate.
Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.

Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?

When Perseverance previously encountered silica-rich rocks on the inner rim of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.

articles.title: Glass Behaves Strangely When Stretched to One Atom Wide – the Discovery Could Transform Electronics
articles.dek: As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.
paragraphs: As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.

Glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs. It insulates windows, protects buildings from temperature changes, and helps keep electronic components separated. Yet when researchers reduced glass to a thread just one atom wide, they found it could transmit heat with remarkable efficiency, revealing an unexpected behavior that could reshape how engineers approach increasingly small electronics.

In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology , researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps. Each step carried exactly 40% of the maximum heat a single channel can transmit under the laws of quantum physics. The observation marks the first time researchers have detected this kind of quantized heat flow carried by atomic vibrations.

The finding could help address a growing challenge in electronics. As components become smaller and more powerful, managing the heat they generate becomes increasingly difficult. Glass, in the form of silicon dioxide, is widely used as an insulating layer in computer chips, making its behavior at extremely small scales particularly relevant.

“We will eventually reach a bottleneck to design the next generation of electronic and photonic devices,” said Longji Cui, an assistant professor in the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder. “Thermal management inside electronic devices is extremely important, but to do it more effectively, we need to understand how heat is flowing through these nanoscale devices.”

Ordinary glass is a poor conductor of heat because its atoms are arranged in a disordered structure. That disorder scatters the vibrations that carry heat through the material, making it difficult for thermal energy to travel efficiently. When researchers stretched the glass into a connection just one atom wide, however, there was no room for the same disorder. Instead, the atomic vibrations could pass through the narrow connection with much less interference.

“Glass is what we put in windows to keep heat in,” said Guilherme de Vilhena, a researcher at the Materials Science Institute of Madrid and a co-author of the study. “But stretch it into a thread one atom wide, and it does the opposite: it lets heat through with an efficiency we had never seen in an insulator.”

The team made the observation using a scanning thermal probe microscope (SThM), an instrument equipped with a glass tip and a built-in thermometer. It measures temperature and heat flow through extremely small contacts by detecting the behavior of atoms and molecules. Cui compares the instrument to a fingertip capable of sensing heat and texture, only scaled down to the nanoscale.

“When you put your own finger to touch a surface, you can feel the texture and the heat,” he said. “With this microscope, we shrink this finger to nanoscale, and it can read the temperature and heat flow through a single atom.”

To observe the phenomenon, the researchers pressed two pieces of glass together and gradually pulled them apart. As the contact stretched and narrowed, it eventually formed a thread only one atom wide before breaking. This allowed the team to examine how heat moved as the connection approached the atomic limit.
The unexpected behavior could extend beyond glass. Cui believes other materials may exhibit similarly surprising thermal properties when examined at the atomic scale.
“We will now be able to study any material we want with this microscope, and there could be constant surprises that come from this instrument,” he said.

The microscope can investigate thermal transport in virtually any material, including metals and insulators. Cui hopes to use it to develop increasingly sensitive sensors capable of measuring phenomena that conventional instruments cannot easily detect.
“I want to push the world record for thermal sensing, which means I need to build more and more sensitive platforms,” he said. “And people will use it to study fundamental thermal problems.”

articles.title: How the US elections and Iran war are influencing the UN’s COP31 climate talks – and discussions around fossil fuels
articles.dek: The 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact.
paragraphs: The 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change and from one of the worst global energy crises in history. A U. N. report found that global warming will overshoot 1. 5 degrees Celsius (2. 7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change.
The Middle East conflict has intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility , pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters.
Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better.

In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid more than US$12 billion in fossil fuel imports before the U. S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country more than $6 billion more by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and more on solar energy for electricity than most European countries, kept electricity prices lower and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s.

In formal negotiations and in meetings around the U. N. ’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda , countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy.

I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and senior fellow at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the Trump administration’s pressure to get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change , I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives.

A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of 35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035 – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on.

Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries $400 billion a year , according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to three times farther than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by up to 55% by 2035 .

However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least 78% of the electricity powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1. 5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal.
Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes.

Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide technical support to one another , as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and financial help to countries that need it.

The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions.
The world saw this notably with the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the biggest Democratic congressional victory in the United States in over three decades.

Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, called on the COP31 presidents to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a transition away from fossil fuels . He announced that Brazil will host a future conference on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu.

Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its greatest one-year reduction in deforestation and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and provide the $1. 3 trillion in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis.
We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and U. N. Secretary-General António Guterres to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of 18 members of the U. S. House of Representatives also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has pulled the U. S. out of the U. N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and dozens of other international organizations and treaties . The U. S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks.
As former U. S. climate envoy John Kerry said in Antalya , “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.”

The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U. S. climate science after the Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts , and whether it will restore critical funding to international efforts dealing with climate change.

At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries that are likely to lose from such a transition are also working diligently to slow this transition . On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement.

For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens.

articles.title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
articles.dek: For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements.
paragraphs: For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements.

The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position.

“Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.”

The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources.

In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole.

NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time.

The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U. S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

articles.title: A Superheated Plasma Zone Could Explain How Black Holes Launch Powerful Jets
articles.dek: By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to…
paragraphs: By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.

Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light. According to conventional models, these two behaviors should be difficult to sustain together. Rapidly feeding black holes are expected to develop cold, flat disks of swirling matter that make it harder for powerful jets to form.

Scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle. Their observations suggest that a region of extremely hot plasma near the black hole creates conditions in which magnetic fields can help launch a relativistic jet, even as large amounts of matter continue falling inward.

The research, led by Associate Professor Hirofumi Noda of Tohoku University and Associate Professor Kazuhiro Hada of Nagoya City University, combined X-ray measurements with detailed radio observations to investigate both the material surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from its vicinity.

“By looking at the same black hole with state-of-the-art X-ray and radio telescopes, we were able to see both the hot plasma surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from it,” says Noda. “This allows us to directly connect the extreme environment near the black hole with the formation of the jet.”

Located in the constellation Taurus, 3C 120 is an active galaxy whose central supermassive black hole is rapidly accumulating matter while producing a powerful jet. Observations from the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) indicate that the black hole’s cold accretion disk does not extend all the way inward. Instead, its inner edge lies at a distance of approximately 20 times the black hole’s radius. Closer to the black hole, the disk gives way to a flow of plasma heated to hundreds of millions of degrees.

To investigate the structure of the accretion disk, the researchers examined an iron emission line detected by XRISM. The intense gravity near a black hole changes the energies of X-rays emitted by orbiting material, producing a characteristic distortion in the line’s shape. By analyzing this distortion using Einstein’s theory of general relativity, the team estimated how far inward the cold disk extends.

The researchers then used observations from the Global Millimeter VLBI Array, Very Long Baseline Array, and East Asian VLBI Network to examine the jet. These networks combine signals from widely separated radio telescopes, allowing astronomers to resolve structures too small for individual telescopes to distinguish. The measurements traced the jet’s narrowing structure back toward a launching region within the hot plasma flow close to the black hole.

Together, the X-ray and radio observations provide evidence that the black hole’s inner environment differs substantially from the cold, flat disk expected under rapid accretion. Rather than extending uninterrupted toward the black hole, the cooler material transitions into an extremely hot plasma flow in the region associated with the jet’s origin.

The hot plasma could help explain how a rapidly feeding black hole generates such an energetic outflow. Unlike a cold, thin accretion disk, this type of flow may allow strong magnetic fields to build up near the black hole. Those fields can potentially extract energy from the black hole’s rotation and direct it into a concentrated jet of plasma traveling at relativistic speeds.

This mechanism offers a possible explanation for the simultaneous rapid accretion and powerful jet observed in 3C 120. The measurements establish that the system has physical conditions consistent with the proposed process, although they do not directly demonstrate that rotational energy is being extracted to power the jet.

The findings also provide a way to examine how the structure of material surrounding a black hole relates to jet formation. By studying X-ray emissions from the accretion flow alongside high-resolution radio measurements of the jet, researchers can test whether similar conditions occur in other active galaxies.

The team is now extending its investigation to a more massive black hole using coordinated observations from XRISM and radio observatories around the world. They are also comparing the measurements with theoretical models and computer simulations to better understand how matter behaves under extreme gravity.

articles.title: A Strange Black Hole Gap Could Reveal Stars That Died Without Exploding
articles.dek: An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.
paragraphs: An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.

Some massive stars may end their lives without a supernova, collapsing directly into black holes instead of producing a brilliant explosion. A new Caltech-led study suggests that gravitational waves from colliding black holes may contain evidence of these silent stellar deaths, potentially explaining why certain black holes are far more common than others.

Using observations from the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA gravitational-wave network, researchers analyzed 257 black hole mergers recorded over the past decade. They found a pronounced concentration of black holes with masses around 10 times that of the Sun, accounting for roughly three-quarters of the merger sample. Black holes between 12 and 16 solar masses, however, were unexpectedly scarce.

The researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes spin, a property influenced by the processes that formed them. Black holes near 10 solar masses had a narrower distribution of spin rates than the overall population. Combined with the unusual mass distribution, this suggests they may belong to a distinct group with a shared formation history.

“We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time,” says Isaac Legred (PhD ’25), the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who conducted the research at Caltech. “But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.”

Massive stars typically end their lives when their cores collapse and trigger supernova explosions, ejecting much of their material into space. The remaining cores can become neutron stars or black holes. However, theoretical models predict that some massive stars may collapse directly into these compact objects without producing a bright supernova.

Such events, known as failed supernovae, have not yet been conclusively confirmed. Scientists have proposed that they could produce many of the black holes observed in merging binary systems, particularly those around 10 solar masses. In these systems, one or both black holes may have formed through a quiet stellar collapse rather than an explosive death.

“A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun,” says Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and LIGO team member who led the research. “Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin—they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.”

The National Science Foundation (NSF)-funded LIGO observatories in Louisiana and Washington made the first direct detection of gravitational waves from merging black holes in 2015. These ripples in spacetime carry information about the masses and spins of the objects that produced them. Together with Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan, the network has now detected more than 300 black hole collisions.

The new study, published in Physical Review D , was led by Chatziioannou, with Legred as lead author and former Caltech researcher Jacob Golomb (PhD ’25), now at Asari AI, as a coauthor. Although the findings agree with theoretical predictions for failed supernovae, they do not directly establish that these events occurred.

“We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it’s challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky,” Legred says. “With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.”

articles.title: A Deadly Brain Disorder Has Baffled Doctors for Years. Researchers May Have Finally Solved the Mystery
articles.dek: Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering new hope for earlier detection and answers to…
paragraphs: Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering new hope for earlier detection and answers to previously unexplained tragedies.

Some newborns enter the world with devastating brain abnormalities that can cause seizures, profound developmental difficulties, and life-threatening complications. The damage begins before birth, and for some families, the condition has claimed the lives of multiple children without doctors being able to explain why or determine whether it could happen again.

Researchers have now identified a genetic cause behind some of these cases, offering long-awaited answers to affected families. A study published in Genome Medicine links changes in a gene called VPS25 to a previously unknown brain disorder, giving doctors a new way to investigate severe neurological conditions that have remained unexplained.

The discovery began with a pattern of illness shared by children from five unrelated families across Saudi Arabia, Europe, and North America. Three families were initially identified through genomic programs in Saudi Arabia, and researchers subsequently connected their cases with others overseas. Although the families were unrelated, their children had similar symptoms and changes in the same gene.

“When a condition is this rare, one family alone may not be enough to reveal what is happening,” said Professor Fowzan Alkuraya, clinical genetics lead on the study who is affiliated with both King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center (KFSHRC) and King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). “Bringing together clinical experience with genomic data from Saudi Arabia, and connecting it with cases internationally, allowed us to see a pattern that had previously been invisible. This is why building these genomic resources matters: they can help us find answers to diseases that might otherwise remain unexplained.”

To understand how these genetic changes might affect the developing brain, scientists at KAUST examined biological processes inside affected cells. The VPS25 gene plays a role in maintaining nerve cells, and laboratory testing revealed disruptions that altered both the number and contents of tiny packages released by cells. Some of these packages were missing proteins involved in protecting and maintaining nerve cells, offering clues about how the disorder develops.

The findings provide the first evidence connecting VPS25 changes to a human disease. Establishing that connection required clinicians at KFSHRC to work closely with affected families, documenting their symptoms and investigating possible genetic causes, while KAUST researchers studied the underlying cellular problems.

For families who have endured years of uncertainty, identifying the cause offers something that was previously missing: an explanation for their children’s illness and information that could help guide future pregnancy decisions. The discovery also gives clinicians a new gene to examine when investigating similar brain abnormalities and may allow the condition to be detected through genetic testing during pregnancy.

“Knowing that this disease has a rare genetic cause can bring comfort to families who have lived for years with uncertainty about their tragic losses,” said Professor Jasmeen Merzaban, co-lead of the study at KAUST. “It also enables clinicians around the world to recognize similar cases and detect the disease through genetic testing during pregnancy.”

Researchers hope that identifying VPS25 as a disease-associated gene will help uncover additional cases around the world. Studying more affected families could reveal how the condition varies between children, improve diagnosis and genetic counseling, and provide a clearer understanding of how disruptions involving VPS25 interfere with early brain development.

M. from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), including Faculty Baseline Research Funding Program award number 1005 and KAUST Center of Excellence for Smart Health award number 5932. The contributions of the NIH author(s) are considered Works of the United States Government.

articles.title: Type 2 Diabetes Linked to a 53% Higher Risk of Alzheimer’s, Massive Study Finds
articles.dek: A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.
paragraphs: A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.

People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major research review involving data from more than 27 million study participants. The findings strengthen evidence linking diabetes to Alzheimer’s and provide new estimates of how frequently the disease develops among people with the condition.

The Curtin University -led systematic review and meta-analysis examined 40 studies and found that approximately five new cases of Alzheimer’s occur annually for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes. Unlike earlier reviews that often grouped different forms of diabetes and dementia together, the researchers focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease.

The researchers screened 9,431 scientific articles before selecting 40 studies with a combined total of more than 27 million data points, calculated from unadjusted sample sizes. Of these, 23 studies provided information on Alzheimer’s incidence, while 26 examined the association between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s risk.

The pooled incidence was 4. 71 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years. After accounting for other factors included in the original studies’ statistical analyses, people with type 2 diabetes had a 53% higher relative risk of developing Alzheimer’s than those without diabetes. The findings demonstrate an association, not a direct causal relationship.

Studies using administrative health records reported an average of 4. 00 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years, compared with 10. 24 cases in studies using other methods to identify diagnoses. The substantial difference suggests that how Alzheimer’s is identified can influence reported incidence rates.

Among people with type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s incidence was numerically higher in women than men, at 3. 62 versus 2. 76 cases per 1,000 person-years. However, the relative risk associated with diabetes was similar between sexes, with increases of 73% in women and 76% in men. Additional analyses generally supported the overall findings, although incidence estimates varied considerably across studies.

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, said the research provides a more precise assessment of Alzheimer’s risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

“While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease and estimated how often new cases occurred,” Dr. Adewuyi said.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.”

articles.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Jim Mirandy
articles.dek: The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life.
paragraphs: The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life.
Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making.

Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA.

“Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.”

His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space.

By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards.

As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe.

Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center.

Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis.

“My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.”

A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue.
This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him.
A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes.
“Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy.
